content: Children aged 1 to 5 years who are enrolled in Medicaid are at a significantly higher risk of having elevated blood lead levels (BLLs). Data from the National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey (NHANES) from 1991 to 1994 revealed that 83% of U.S. children in this age group with BLLs of 20 µg/dL or higher were Medicaid enrollees. Despite federal requirements mandating blood lead screening for children in the Medicaid program, approximately 81% of these children have not undergone such testing. This lack of screening has resulted in the failure to identify and treat the majority of children with elevated BLLs, leaving them without necessary medical care or environmental interventions. The Advisory Committee on Childhood Lead Poisoning Prevention (ACCLPP) has issued recommendations to address this issue. Health-care providers and health plans are urged to comply with federal laws by conducting blood lead screening, providing diagnostic and treatment services, and referring children with elevated BLLs for environmental and public health follow-up. States should also monitor screening rates and BLLs among Medicaid-enrolled children and implement innovative strategies in areas where traditional screening methods have been inadequate. Elevated BLLs, even as low as 10 µg/dL, are associated with adverse effects on cognitive development, growth, and behavior in children aged 1 to 5 years. Extremely high BLLs (≥70 µg/dL) can lead to severe health outcomes, including seizures, coma, and death. Because children with BLLs in the range of 10-25 µg/dL often do not exhibit clinical symptoms, screening is essential to identify those who require medical or environmental interventions to reduce their BLLs. The ACCLPP has outlined specific recommendations for health-care providers. All children enrolled in Medicaid should receive blood lead screening tests at 12 and 24 months of age. Children aged 36 to 72 months who have not been previously screened should also be tested. Risk assessment questionnaires are not an acceptable substitute for blood lead tests under Medicaid requirements. Screening at both 1 and 2 years of age is critical, as BLLs tend to peak between 18 and 24 months. Identifying elevated BLLs at age 1 can prevent further increases, and rescreening at age 2 is necessary because BLLs may rise even if they were below 10 µg/dL at age 1. Children identified with elevated BLLs require comprehensive follow-up care, including medical management, environmental investigation, and public health case management. While few children will have BLLs high enough to necessitate intensive medical treatment such as chelation therapy, many will require ongoing monitoring, environmental hazard control, and coordination of care. Public health and environmental agencies often play a key role in providing these services. The ACCLPP also provides recommendations for states and agencies administering Medicaid programs. Medicaid managed-care contracts should explicitly include these requirements and provide for follow-up services for children with elevated BLLs. States should also educate health-care providers about Medicaid blood lead screening policies and the scientific basis for these guidelines. Environmental follow-up is a critical component of case management for children with elevated BLLs. Federal law entitles Medicaid-enrolled children to all necessary follow-up services, including environmental investigations. However, many states have not established reimbursement mechanisms for these services, and only a limited number of states currently cover environmental investigations or case management under Medicaid. Collaboration between Medicaid agencies and other programs serving children, such as the Special Supplemental Nutrition Program for Women, Infants, and Children (WIC) and Head Start, can help increase screening rates and improve access to preventive care. The use of new blood lead screening technologies, such as hand-held testing devices, can further enhance screening services by providing immediate results and reducing delays in follow-up care. Despite the federal mandate for universal blood lead screening of Medicaid-enrolled children, compliance remains low. During 1991-1994, an estimated 535,000 children aged 1 to 5 years in the Medicaid program had elevated BLLs, yet 352,000 of these children were never screened or treated. This represents a missed opportunity to identify and assist children at high risk for lead poisoning.
